The man who jumped off Everest

By: Graham Coetzer | Paid

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
South African Pierre Carter has become the first person to legally paraglide off the summit of Mount Everest - a feat few could ever dream of achieving.

Unique Selling Point:
Climbing Mount Everest is one of the most dangerous tests of man vs nature. But for a certain type of person, there are even grander adventures to be had . Enter 55 year old South African, Pierre Carter, who has taken the rapidly growing extreme sport known as "climb and fly" to new heights. Earlier this year, Pierre spent around R600 000 from his life savings to fund the adventure of a lifetime to the Himalaya's, where he successfully climbed to about 800m below the summit of Mount Everest (the height the Nepalese government permitted him to fly from) before jumping of the side of the mountain with his paraglider - successfully landing about 20 minutes later. He became the first person in history to do so legally, paving the way for future adventure sports fanatics.

Summary:
Carter is in the process of completing what he calls his "7Summits7Flights" project. Similar to the dreams of many mountain climbers to climb the seven highest mountains on the seven continents, Carter has added the Adrenaline rush of paragliding off each one. So far he's recieved little media` coverage for his exploits, and even fewer sponsorships - the soft spoken building contractor has chosen to for the most part go it alone. With Everest in the bag, he only has the highest mountain in Antarctica left to complete his mission. Carter was an avid mountain climber before getting into paragliding. Eventually he became a competitor in the elite X-Alps Extreme Sports event, where athletes race across the Alps by foot and paraglider - before he came up with the 7Sumits7Flights concept.

Further information:
Treatment:
At it's heart this is an adventure story. I want to stay away from boring sit down interviews and experts as much as possible. And the footage of Carter's exploits, if handled correctly, speaks for itself
We have organised with Pierre to take our presenter on a tandem paragliding flight from a mountain near Hartebeespoort Dam. I was thinking of using either Mac or Derek, but since Derek has already done a tandem paragliding flight I think we would get a much better response from Mac (who has agreed to do it). So the flight with our presenter is one layer. The next layer is to use Pierre's footage (which he has a lot of) to really build the drama around the adventure of climbing Everest and then Paragliding from it. There are lots of elements of drama here, spending weeks at base camp to acclimatize his body to the conditions, practice climbs, logistics of hauling the gear up, to crossing the deadly ice flows where hundreds of climbers have lost their lives, the hopes that the weather conditions would be absolutely perfect to allow for the flight, the difficulties of getting in the air and staying their at those kinds of heights where the air is very thin, and then the majestic footage of the successful flight. The third layer is to weave in some of his past exploits, him at home as husband and father, this very normal guy with an extraordinary dream. And then finally, South Africa has a bit of a name in the world of paragliding, a South African was the first person ever to set the world record for the longest paraglide - at a distance of over 500km - and with people like Carter following in those exploits, we have a lot to be proud of.

Script:


The Man Who Jumped Off Everest
First Draft Script
05 July 2022

Intro Music

Upsound Pierre
Mac: Ok, at what point do I need my helmet? I feel like I need it right now.

Pierre: No, no. Only just before we take off, and you’re clipped in, then we put the helmet on. Ok?

Mac: Ok, so we basically attach here, I sit there in front, I don’t have a reserve, you guys note that? I don’t have a reserve.

Pierre: Ja, I have the reserve.

Link Mac
55-year-old South African Pierre Carter is a man that dreams big - not only does he want to climb the seven highest mountains in the seven continents, he also wants to paraglide off them. Crazy right?

Voice
Speaking of crazy, I’m joining this paragliding adventurer for a tandem flight near Hartebeespoort. That’s if we actually get into the air.

Upsound Pierre
Pierre: If it’s not flying we’re just going to go boom, and I’ll then land on top of you, and I’ll be fine and you’ll be in the rocks, might be a bit bruised and battered…

Mac: Thanks, cut guys! Cut! Cut!

Voice
In reality, I was in very good hands. Pierre, who is a springbok paraglider, has thousands of flying hours under his belt. Not just that, he’s had an encounter with the world’s highest and probably deadliest mountain - Mount Everest.

Upsound Mac
I’ve got a huge, huge fear for heights, but hey man it is what it is, let’s go.

Upsound take off and Mac in air

Upsound Mac
This is the most amazing thing ever.

Upsound Pierre
Mac: Outside of jumping off mountains, what other stuff do you do?

Pierre: I’m just your average guy, and I run a little building company, I’ve got my wife and I’ve got my daughter who’s 26, and we’ve got four Border Collies.

Voice
He’s at his happiest joining the Cape vulture colonies around Hartebeespoort mid flight, or spending hours in the air navigating the Drakensberg mountains.

And his passion has led to the adventure of a lifetime, a daring plan he calls 7summits7flights. The project entails not only climbing the seven highest peaks on the world’s seven continents, but also paragliding off them at the same time. And he’s funding it all, from his own pocket.

In April this year, he set off to the Himalayas and his biggest challenge to date…

Link Mac
Combining the extremes of mountain climbing and paragliding is no easy feat, but on top of that is an even bigger challenge, getting the authorities to play along.

Voice
It took Pierre and fellow enthusiasts years to get permission to fly off Kilimanjaro, Africa’s highest mountain.

Upsound Pierre
Pierre: That took us 10 years to get that permit.

Mac: 10 years?

Pierre: Ten years of knocking on the door.

Voice
With Everest, a local tour operator named Dawa Steven Sherpa was able to secure permission for Pierre’s jump from the Nepalese government - something they’d never allowed before.

Sound Up Dawa Sherpa
They said, you know, Covid has been such a bad time for the whole country, let’s do something that would really make a splash, and put Nepal in the right light, so everything aligned and we in the end managed to get the permit.

Voice
With the paperwork out of the way, the real challenge began. Hundreds of people have lost their lives attempting to summit Everest. Just getting to base camp, at a height of 5364 metres, takes 10 days as climbers have to acclimatise their bodies to the thin air.

Upsound Dawa Steven Sherpa
You know the altitude itself is a killer, right? If you were to helicopter into the Everest region, just even to base camp, if you’d just come from the beach in South Africa, within a matter of a few hours you’d probably be dead.

Voice
Long time friend and fellow paraglider Jeremy Holdcroft joined Pierre’s expedition up to base camp.

Upsound Jeremy
And just staying at base camp, I mean that was… Base camp was pretty tough. I mean the temperature swings were drastic, we had -20 during the night.

Upsound Pierre Base Camp
Base camp wash day.

Voice
One of the deadliest sections on the way to the summit, is the notorious Khumbu Icefall.

Upsound Pierre
Pierre: So you’re walking around blocks of ice, I mean they are..

Mac: Huge

Pierre: Huge, like 4 storey blocks.

Voice
This area is so dangerous, that a group of local guides have to assist climbers by mapping out the route, and setting up life saving equipment along the way.

Upsound Pierre
And they have a group called the ice fall doctors, that set ropes up all the way through the ice fall.

And the crevasse is a hundred metres deep or more, you can’t see the bottom of them on some of them. And some of them you have to jump across, you know they sort of a metre, metre and a half, some of them are three metres and then they put a ladder across - the icefall doctors that carry up these aluminium ladders and put them there.

Voice
As the ascent continues, the air gets constantly thinner, and simply breathing becomes a difficult task.

Sound Up Pierre in tent
Chilling at seven thousand, two, three hundred metres I think it is.

Sound Up Pierre
If you can do a marathon, and you can do three marathons in a row, it still doesn’t mean you can get up Everest. It still got to me, the amount of time waiting around, and the slowness that it takes for your body to acclimatise.

Voice
After an arduous journey, climbers eventually reach camp iv, the final stop before they’ll attempt to summit. It’s an area with an infamous reputation.

Upsound Pierre
And 8000 metres, so it’s just in what they call the death zone, where your body is essentially dying slowly.

Voice
Most people will have to take supplemental oxygen at this altitude and the thin air poses even more problems to would be paragliders…

Sound Up Jeremy
Up there the air is very, very thin, you have to know exactly what you are doing.

Voice
On a clear Everest morning, 8 weeks after starting his trek up the mountain, Pierre was ready to fly into the record books.

Upsound Pierre take off

Voice
On the 15th of May, 2022, Pierre Carter became the first person in the world to legally paraglide off Mount Everest.

Upsound Pierre in the air.
It was, an elation went through me, you think thank God I am actually going to fly off this mountain.

So I’ve been on big mountains, but these are, the Himalayas are big…they are huge… You’re flying through history in a way.

Voice
After experiencing the Himalayas in a way the rest of us can only dream of, he landed safely. And his first words on a world first were characteristically modest.

Upsound Pierre Landing
At least that’s over, whoo hoo.

Voice
Back in Harties my own safe landing was, well, a little louder.

Upsound Mac
Landed! What a jol, what a jol. This is abolutely amazing, I can’t even begin to explain it to anyone, what this feels like. You know you’re soaring above with the birds, it’s, it’s surreal.

Link Mac
You might think pulling off the Everest expedition was the climax, it doesn’t get more challenging than that. But Pierre’s got one more climb. You want to guess which mountain that is?

Voice
Mount Vinson is the highest mountain in Antarctica, and also the remotest location of the seven summits. But Pierre is determined to not let either the staggering price tag, of nearly R900 000, or anything else, stand in his way.

Upsound Pierre
Pierre: I’ve always said that when you get to 85, you must see how many body parts you’ve replaced. Then you know you’ve lived it.

Mac: You’ve really lived right?

END

Promo 1 (21sec)
Upsound Mac
Mac: So whenever you go up a mountain do you ever hear the song - Ain’t no mountain high enough? (6sec)

Voice
We take to the skies to meet the man living the adventure of a lifetime…

Upsound Pierre take off Everest

Voice
South African Pierre Carter has flown into the history books by becoming the first person to legally climb and paraglide off Mount Everest.

Upsound Pierre Fly Everest



Promo 2 (21sec)
Voice
We take to the skies with Springbok paraglider Pierre Carter.

Upsound Mac
Mac: Thanks, cut guys! Cut! Cut!

Sound Up Mac Fly

Voice
And find out the story behind the man who flew off Everest…

Sound Up Fly Everest





Promo 3 (11sec)
Voice
His plan is to not only climb the seven highest mountains on the 7 continents, but also paraglide off them. We meet the man who flew off Everest.

Upsound Pierre Everest Flight

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): South African Pierre Carter has become the first person to legally paraglide off the summit of Mount Everest - a feat few could ever dream of achieving.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: Climbing Mount Everest is one of the most dangerous tests of man vs nature. But for a certain type of person, there are even grander adventures to be had . Enter 55 year old South African, Pierre Carter, who has taken the rapidly growing extreme sport known as "climb and fly" to new heights. Earlier this year, Pierre spent around R600 000 from his life savings to fund the adventure of a lifetime to the Himalaya's, where he successfully climbed to about 800m below the summit of Mount Everest (the height the Nepalese government permitted him to fly from) before jumping of the side of the mountain with his paraglider - successfully landing about 20 minutes later. He became the first person in history to do so legally, paving the way for future adventure sports fanatics.
metadata.Summary: Carter is in the process of completing what he calls his "7Summits7Flights" project. Similar to the dreams of many mountain climbers to climb the seven highest mountains on the seven continents, Carter has added the Adrenaline rush of paragliding off each one. So far he's recieved little media` coverage for his exploits, and even fewer sponsorships - the soft spoken building contractor has chosen to for the most part go it alone. With Everest in the bag, he only has the highest mountain in Antarctica left to complete his mission. Carter was an avid mountain climber before getting into paragliding. Eventually he became a competitor in the elite X-Alps Extreme Sports event, where athletes race across the Alps by foot and paraglider - before he came up with the 7Sumits7Flights concept.
metadata.Further information: Treatment: At it's heart this is an adventure story. I want to stay away from boring sit down interviews and experts as much as possible. And the footage of Carter's exploits, if handled correctly, speaks for itself We have organised with Pierre to take our presenter on a tandem paragliding flight from a mountain near Hartebeespoort Dam. I was thinking of using either Mac or Derek, but since Derek has already done a tandem paragliding flight I think we would get a much better response from Mac (who has agreed to do it). So the flight with our presenter is one layer. The next layer is to use Pierre's footage (which he has a lot of) to really build the drama around the adventure of climbing Everest and then Paragliding from it. There are lots of elements of drama here, spending weeks at base camp to acclimatize his body to the conditions, practice climbs, logistics of hauling the gear up, to crossing the deadly ice flows where hundreds of climbers have lost their lives, the hopes that the weather conditions would be absolutely perfect to allow for the flight, the difficulties of getting in the air and staying their at those kinds of heights where the air is very thin, and then the majestic footage of the successful flight. The third layer is to weave in some of his past exploits, him at home as husband and father, this very normal guy with an extraordinary dream. And then finally, South Africa has a bit of a name in the world of paragliding, a South African was the first person ever to set the world record for the longest paraglide - at a distance of over 500km - and with people like Carter following in those exploits, we have a lot to be proud of.
